public_rationale: All four named companies have evidence that subscription users consumed compute costing more than they paid, with the company covering the gap. GitHub's product chief said GitHub 'absorbed much of the escalating inference cost' under its fixed-price plans (e1). Anthropic said one user consumed 'tens of thousands' in model usage on a $200 plan (e2). Sam Altman said OpenAI was losing money on $200 Pro subscriptions because of heavy use (e3). TechCrunch reported, citing unnamed sources, that Cursor still lost money on individual developer accounts in April 2026 (e4). A rebuttal argues Anthropic's real serving cost is far below list price, but it still estimates a loss on the heaviest users (e5). That challenges how big the subsidy was, not whether it existed. The phrase 'every other AI company' cannot be checked and is not scored.
limitations: Only the four named companies were tested; the universal 'every other AI company' is unverified.
Evidence of losses mostly concerns heavy users and comes from company statements or news reports, not audited per-user cost data.
Size depends on valuing tokens at list price versus actual serving cost; 'way, way more' may overstate the gap at actual cost for Anthropic (e5).
GitHub's statement is quoted through ITPro, and the Cursor report relies on anonymous sources.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor and every other AI company have been subsidizing compute, letting users consume far more in tokens than their subscriptions cost.

statement.excerpt: Much like Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor, and every other AI company, Microsoft has been subsidizing the cost of compute, allowing users to burn way, way more in tokens than their subscriptions cost.
statement.document_title: Exclusive: Microsoft To Shift GitHub Copilot Users To Token-Based Billing, Tighten Rate Limits

from_speaker: Much like Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor, and every other AI company
Microsoft has been subsidizing the cost of compute
allowing users to burn way, way more in tokens than their subscriptions cost
our_interpretation: Plain reading: under flat-rate subscription plans, each named company let at least some subscribers use tokens whose cost exceeded what they paid, so the company covered the gap. The claim does not say every user was unprofitable. The heavy-user reading is fair to the speaker, and reviewers accepted it.

'Cost' is read as either the company's own stated losses or absorbed costs on subscription users, or credible reports of the same. A dollar value at list API prices alone counts only as weaker support. Where it matters, reports of the actual cost of serving users are preferred.

'Has been' describes an ongoing state up to the post date with no start named. I use the flat-rate AI and coding-agent subscription era leading up to the post: 2025-01-01 to 2026-04-20. The window is not limited to a single month.

'Every other AI company' is a sweeping generalization that cannot be checked company by company. The test covers the four named firms (Microsoft/GitHub, Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor). The universal part is flagged, not scored.
No dollar figure, metric or accounting basis is claimed. This is treated as a qualitative claim about pricing practice, not a specific financial metric, so metric_scope is null.
criteria.support_condition: For each named company, a company statement or credible report from the period shows that subscription users could consume, or did consume, compute costing more than their subscription fee, with the company absorbing the difference or losing money on those subscribers.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evidence that one or more of the named companies did not absorb compute costs above subscription prices during the period. Examples: a company reports its subscription plans were profitable even for its heaviest users, or its plans already charged users the full token cost.

evidence.excerpt: "GitHub has absorbed much of the escalating inference cost behind that usage, but the current premium request model is no longer sustainable."
evidence.locator: paragraphs 6-7, quoting GitHub CPO Mario Rodriguez
evidence.explanation: GitHub's product chief says GitHub absorbed rising inference costs under fixed-price Copilot plans. That is Microsoft subsidizing compute beyond what subscriptions charged. The quote describes the state before the April 2026 change.

evidence.excerpt: “One user consumed tens of thousands in model usage on a $200 plan,” the company noted.
evidence.explanation: Anthropic itself said a $200-a-month subscriber used model usage worth tens of thousands of dollars, far more than the plan price.

evidence.excerpt: "Insane thing: We are currently losing money on OpenAI Pro subscriptions!" he wrote in a post.
evidence.explanation: OpenAI's CEO said the $200 Pro subscription lost money because people used it more than expected, so usage cost more than the price.

evidence.excerpt: the company has reached positive gross margins on its sales to large enterprises, but continues to lose money on individual developer accounts, according to one person.
evidence.explanation: Anonymous-source report that Cursor still lost money on individual subscribers just before the post, after earlier negative gross margins overall.

evidence.excerpt: If a heavy Claude Code Max user consumes $5,000 worth of tokens at Anthropic's retail API prices, and the actual compute cost is roughly 10% of that, Anthropic is looking at approximately $500 in real compute cost for the heaviest users.
evidence.explanation: Disputes how large Anthropic's subsidy is, arguing actual serving cost is about 10% of list price. Even so, it estimates a loss of about $300 a month on the heaviest users, so it weakens the size of the subsidy, not its existence.

evidence.excerpt: Though most users’ costs have stayed fairly constant, the hardest requests cost an order of magnitude more than simple ones. API-based pricing is the best way to reflect that.
evidence.locator: section 'Why did we change the plan?'
evidence.explanation: Cursor explains that flat request pricing let hard requests cost far more than they were charged, which is why it moved Pro to usage-based pricing in mid-2025.
